x.ASV: A Song of Ascents. Blessed is every one that feareth Jehovah, That walketh in his ways.
x.Darby: A Song of degrees. Blessed is every one that feareth Jehovah, that walketh in his ways.
x.KJV: A Song of degrees. Blessed is every one that feareth the Lord; that walketh in his ways.
x.YLT: A Song of the Ascents. O the happiness of every one fearing Jehovah, Who is walking in His ways.

nt: The psalmist is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How happy is everyone fearing Yahweh] or [Truly blessed is everyone who fears Yahweh]

The psalmist is speaking of a person who obeys Yahweh as if that person were **walking** along Yahweh’s **ways**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one living according to his commands]

x.ASV: For thou shalt eat the labor of thy hands: Happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee.
x.Darby: For thou shalt eat the labour of thy hands; happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee.
x.KJV: For thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands: happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee.
x.YLT: The labour of thy hands thou surely eatest, Happy art thou, and good is to thee.

nt: Here, **labor of your palms** represents the result of the work done with someone’s hands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The results of your work]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **happiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [makes you happy]

x.ASV: Thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine, In the innermost parts of thy house; Thy children like olive plants, Round about thy table.
x.Darby: Thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine in the inner part of thy house; thy children like olive-plants round about thy table.
x.KJV: Thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine by the sides of thine house: thy children like olive plants round about thy table.
x.YLT: Thy wife is as a fruitful vine in the sides of thy house, Thy sons as olive plants around thy table.

nt: The point of this comparison is that just as a **fruitful vine** produces much fruit, so the man’s **wife** will have many children. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Your wife will have many children]

The point of this comparison is that just as **shoots of olive trees** are vigorous and healthy, so the man’s **sons** will be strong and thriving. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Your sons will be strong and healthy]

Here the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense that includes both male and female children. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [Your sons and daughters]

x.ASV: Behold, thus shall the man be blessed That feareth Jehovah.
x.Darby: Behold, thus shall the man be blessed that feareth Jehovah.
x.KJV: Behold, that thus shall the man be blessed that feareth the Lord.
x.YLT: Lo, surely thus is the man blessed who is fearing Jehovah.

nt: The psalmist is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Indeed]

The expression **will be blessed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will bless the man who fears him]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [everyone]

x.ASV: Jehovah bless thee out of Zion: And see thou the good of Jerusalem all the days of thy life.
x.Darby: Jehovah will bless thee out of Zion; and mayest thou see the good of Jerusalem all the days of thy life,
x.KJV: The Lord shall bless thee out of Zion: and thou shalt see the good of Jerusalem all the days of thy life.
x.YLT: Jehovah doth bless thee out of Zion, Look, then, on the good of Jerusalem, All the days of thy life,

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **good**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that you might see Jerusalem prospering]

x.ASV: Yea, see thou thy children’s children. Peace be upon Israel.
x.Darby: And see thy children's children. Peace be upon Israel!
x.KJV: Yea, thou shalt see thy children’s children, and peace upon Israel.
x.YLT: And see the sons of thy sons! Peace on Israel!

nt: Here, **and that** marks **you may see sons to your sons** as a further goal or purpose of Yahweh’s blessing in the previous verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [and also so that you may see]

Here the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense that includes both male and female descendants. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [children of your children]

The psalmist is using **sons to your sons** as a common expression of the culture to mean grandchildren. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [many descendants]

The psalmist is asking Yahweh to bless the people of Israel. In your translation, use a form that people would recognize as a blessing in your language. You might express this as a prayer, if that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh give peace to Israel]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **Peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [May well-being come upon]
